title: Kayla Hamilton Act
official_title: To amend the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008 and the Homeland Security Act of 2002 to enhance efforts to combat the trafficking of children.
summary: The Kayla Hamilton Act tightens the placement process for unaccompanied migrant children in federal custody. It requires the Department of Health and Human Services to place children 12 and older in a secure facility for the duration of any immigration proceedings if they are a flight risk or a danger, including if they have gang-related tattoos or markings, a conviction for a serious criminal offense or aggravated felony, or a gang-related arrest, charge, or conviction. It also prohibits placing any child with an individual who is not a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident, or who — or an adult in whose household — has been convicted of certain sex, trafficking, domestic-violence, child-abuse, murder, or felony offenses, and requires HHS to give DHS detailed background information on all adult household members at any placement home.
brief: Requires secure-facility placement for unaccompanied migrant children 12 and older who are a flight risk or danger — including those with gang-related indicators or serious criminal convictions — bars placement with any individual who is not a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident or who has certain criminal convictions, and mandates sharing of household adult background information with DHS.

top_lines.headline: Secure Facility for Gang-Affiliated Minors
subs: Before placing an unaccompanied child 12 or older, HHS must contact the child's home country consulate or embassy to request any relevant arrest records, pending charges, or conviction documents
HHS must also examine the child for gang-related tattoos and markings

If the child is a flight risk or a danger — including having a gang-related tattoo or marking, a conviction for a serious criminal offense or aggravated felony, or a gang-related arrest, pending charge, or conviction — HHS must place them in a secure facility for the duration of any immigration proceedings

top_lines.headline: Sponsor Vetting Requirements
subs: No child may be placed with any individual who is not a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident, or who — or an adult resident of whose household — has been convicted of certain sex, trafficking, domestic-violence, child-abuse, murder, or felony offenses

Before placement, HHS must share with DHS: names, Social Security or individual taxpayer identification numbers, dates of birth, addresses, immigration status, contact information, and background-check results for all adult residents of the placement household

Required background checks include, at a minimum, an investigation of the Dru Sjodin National Sex Offender Public Website, a public records background check, and a national criminal history background check based on fingerprints for every adult in the household

likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House and was received in the Senate in December 2025, but has only 2 cosponsors and no Senate companion bill visible. Democrats have broadly opposed bills that restrict HHS placement flexibility for unaccompanied migrant children, and the 60-vote threshold for Senate floor consideration makes bipartisan support essential. No Senate committee action has been reported.

items.main: Names the Act the “Kayla Hamilton Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Placement Determinations for Unaccompanied Alien Children

items.main: Amends the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 279(b)(2)) so the Office of Refugee Resettlement Director makes unaccompanied-child placement determinations in accordance with 8 U.S.C. 1232(c)(2).
items.detail: Conforming amendment tying ORR's placement authority to the safe-and-secure-placement standard rewritten by Section 3.

sections.label: Section 3 — Enhancing Efforts to Combat the Trafficking of Children

items.main: Before any placement, HHS must consult with the Secretary of Homeland Security and the Attorney General to help ensure the child appears at immigration hearings, is protected from smugglers, traffickers, and gangs, and to determine flight risk, danger, and criminal history; children in HHS custody are otherwise to be placed in the least restrictive setting in their best interest, and may not be released on their own recognizance.
items.detail: The consultation and least-restrictive-setting rules apply to all unaccompanied children; the consulate-records request, gang examination, and secure-facility placement apply only to children 12 or older.

items.main: For unaccompanied migrant children aged 12 and older, requires HHS to request arrest records, pending charges, and conviction documents from the child's home country consulate or embassy and conduct an examination for gang-related tattoos and markings before making any placement.
items.detail: A child 12 or older must be placed in a secure facility for the duration of any immigration proceedings (and, if ordered removed, until removal) if the child is a flight risk or a danger to self, others, or the community — including having a gang-related tattoo or marking, a conviction for a serious criminal offense or aggravated felony, or, for gang-related conduct, an arrest record, pending charge, other pending proceeding, or conviction. Children younger than 12 are exempt from the gang-screening and consulate-records requirements.

items.main: Prohibits placement of any unaccompanied child with an individual who is not a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident, or who — or an adult resident of whose household — has been convicted of an enumerated offense, and requires HHS to transmit detailed household information to DHS before completing any placement.
items.detail: Required information includes names, Social Security or individual taxpayer identification numbers, dates of birth, addresses, immigration status, contact information, and background-check results for all adult residents of the proposed placement household. Background checks must include, at a minimum, an investigation of the Dru Sjodin National Sex Offender Public Website, a public records background check, and a national criminal history background check based on fingerprints. The enumerated categories of prohibited individuals include those convicted of a sex offense, severe trafficking, domestic violence, child abuse, murder or manslaughter, an aggravated felony, any felony, or any crime punishable by more than 1 year, plus any other offense the Attorney General designates in the Attorney General's sole and unreviewable discretion.

sections.label: Section 5 — Exemption from Paperwork Reduction Act and Administrative Procedure Act

items.main: Provides that nothing in the Act requires DHS, HHS, the State Department, or the Attorney General to comply with the Paperwork Reduction Act or to conduct APA notice-and-comment rulemaking if those officials determine compliance would impede immediate implementation.
items.detail: Lets the implementing agencies bypass Paperwork Reduction Act review (chapter 35 of title 44) and APA rulemaking (subchapter II of chapter 5 of title 5) at their own determination.

items.main: Takes effect on enactment and applies to release and custody determinations that are pending or occur on or after enactment, and to all release redeterminations.
items.detail: Reaches unaccompanied-alien-child cases already in progress at enactment, not only new ones.

underreported.section: Section 5 — Paperwork Reduction Act / Administrative Procedure Act Exemption
underreported.summary: Lets DHS, HHS, the State Department, and the Attorney General skip Paperwork Reduction Act review and Administrative Procedure Act notice-and-comment rulemaking whenever those officials themselves determine that compliance would impede immediate implementation of the Act.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed around gang screening and sponsor vetting, but this separate section removes the ordinary procedural checks on how the new placement rules are implemented, at the agencies' own discretion — a structural change absent from the short title and stated purpose.

gaps: The bill requires HHS to contact a child's home country consulate for a criminal record before placement, but does not establish a timeline for how long HHS may hold a child while awaiting a response, or what happens if the consulate does not respond.

The bill bars placement with any individual who is not a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident but does not address what happens to a child if no eligible placement is available, potentially requiring prolonged secure-facility detention.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Jayapal
featured_quotes.text: let me just remind the majority that the Office of Refugee Resettlement subjects all potential sponsors of unaccompanied kids to an assessment. That assessment includes numerous factors, including the sponsor's relationship to the child, the sponsor's motivation for seeking to care for the child, and any special vulnerabilities that the child has.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Rivas
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, the bill we are debating today is a bad bill. It is a bad bill that will harm vulnerable children, do nothing to fix our immigration system, and embolden Trump to continue wreaking havoc in our communities. Republicans are exploiting a tragedy to push forth a bill that undermines and strips away critical rights and protections for vulnerable children. H.R. 4371 treats immigrant children like criminals and prevents unaccompanied minors from being reunited with their families.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Ramirez
featured_quotes.text: we are less than 10 days away from Christmas, a day in which many celebrate the birth of Jesus, a refugee. In regard to the hypocrisy of those who would quote Scripture asserting the preciousness of children while they pursue new, cruel punishments for child refugees, I find that not just hypocritical but despicable. This administration and the Republicans have used their power not to protect children but, instead, to strip unaccompanied children who come to this country fleeing danger, looking for safety or protection.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Stansbury
featured_quotes.text: Let me begin by saying what should be clear to every Member of this body: The murder of Kayla Hamilton is a horrific and truly heartbreaking tragedy, and no family should ever have to endure such a loss. Nothing that we can do or say here will diminish the pain of those who loved her.

Requirement to transmit household adult background check results to DHS before each placement

added: New Sec. 2 amends the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 279(b)(2)) so ORR placement determinations must follow 8 U.S.C. 1232(c)(2)
New mandatory consultation step with DHS and the Attorney General before any placement, to assess flight risk, danger, and criminal history
Express prohibition on releasing an unaccompanied alien child on his or her own recognizance
Detailed secure-facility placement rules for children 12 or older who are a flight risk or danger, including serious-offense, aggravated-felony, and gang-activity triggers (with INA cross-references)

New subparagraph (D) listing 11 categories of individuals a child may not be placed with, including non-citizens/non-LPRs and those (or household members) convicted of sex, trafficking, domestic violence, child abuse, murder, or felony offenses
New Sec. 5 exempting agencies from the Paperwork Reduction Act and Administrative Procedure Act where compliance would impede immediate implementation

modified: Background-check requirement (paragraph (3)(D)(vii)) renamed the registry to the "Dru Sjodin National Sex Offender Public Website" and now also accepts an individual taxpayer identification number; the introduced version cited the DOJ National Sex Offender public website and required a social security number
Gang/criminal-record screening restructured: child-12-or-younger carve-out replaced with rules applying to children "12 years of age or older"
Bill purpose expanded to also amend the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (introduced amended only the Wilberforce Act)
removed: Introduced text's standalone "a child shall not be placed with an individual who is unlawfully present in the United States" sentence in paragraph (3)(A) is replaced by the broader citizen/LPR requirement in the new (D)
